analogy.p: Imagine a line of shopping trolleys rolling across a smooth floor onto a muddy patch. When one wheel hits the mud first it slows down while the other wheel is still moving fast, so the trolley swings round and changes direction: this is refraction. A convex lens is like a mud patch shaped so that the edge trolleys swing in towards the middle and all meet at the same spot, while a concave lens shapes the mud so trolleys swing outwards. The analogy breaks down because light does not have wheels or friction: it changes direction because the wave speed changes between materials, and the wave front bends rather than a trolley being dragged.
analogy.t: Wheels hitting mud at an angle

bullets: The spec wording covers: the **principal focus**, the **focal length**, **real and virtual images**, **ray diagrams** for convex and concave lenses, and **magnification**.
You must be able to describe the effect of each type of lens on parallel rays of light.
Ray diagrams must show the image formed for an object placed at different distances from a convex lens, and for a concave lens.
Magnification is a **ratio** with no units: magnification = image height / object height.
This content is **Physics only (triple)**; Combined Science students do not need it.
It links to **refraction** (4.6.1), the electromagnetic spectrum (visible light) and to optical devices such as magnifying glasses, cameras and the eye.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Physics (triple science only) asks you to know how convex and concave lenses form images, to draw ray diagrams for both types, to describe the images using the words real, virtual, upright, inverted, magnified and diminished, and to calculate magnification. A **lens** is a piece of transparent material, usually glass or plastic, with curved surfaces that **refracts** light so the rays change direction. The whole topic rests on one idea: refraction at the curved surfaces bends rays, and where the bent rays meet (or appear to meet) an image is formed. Examiners reward ray diagrams drawn with a ruler, with arrows on the rays, and a clearly labelled image.

bullets: The **normal** is an imaginary line at 90 degrees to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
Air to glass: the ray slows down and bends towards the normal. Glass to air: the ray speeds up and bends away from the normal.
A ray travelling along the normal (at 90 degrees to the surface) is **not refracted**: it passes straight through.
At the exact centre of a thin lens the two surfaces are almost parallel, so a ray through the centre emerges essentially **undeviated**; this is why the 'ray through the centre' rule works.
Thicker, more strongly curved lenses bend light more, so they have a **shorter focal length** (a more powerful lens).
In ray diagrams we simplify by drawing the bend as happening **once**, on a straight vertical line through the centre of the lens, rather than at both surfaces.
core.p: A lens works because light changes speed when it passes between materials of different optical density, such as air and glass. When a ray enters glass at an angle, one side of the wavefront slows first, so the ray bends **towards the normal**; when it leaves glass into air it bends **away from the normal**. A lens has curved surfaces, so the angle of incidence is different at each point on the surface, which means different rays are bent by different amounts. This is what lets a lens bring rays together or spread them apart, rather than just shifting them sideways as a rectangular glass block does.

bullets: A convex lens has surfaces that bulge outwards, so it is thicker at the centre.
Parallel rays (for example from a very distant object such as the Sun) are made to **converge** and cross at the **principal focus**.
The principal focus is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after passing through the lens.
A convex lens has **two principal foci**, one on each side, the same distance from the lens, because light can enter from either side.
Convex lenses are used in **magnifying glasses, cameras, projectors, telescopes, microscopes and in spectacles for long sight**.
A convex lens can form both **real** images (on a screen) and **virtual** images (magnifying glass use), depending on where the object is placed.
core.p: A **convex lens** is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It is also called a **converging lens** because it brings parallel rays of light together to a single point. Parallel rays entering the lens are refracted towards the normal at the first surface and again at the second surface, so every ray ends up bent inwards towards the principal axis. The rays that arrive nearer the edge of the lens meet a more steeply sloping surface and are bent more, which is exactly the right amount to make them all cross at the same point.

bullets: A concave lens has surfaces that curve inwards, so it is thinner at the centre and thicker at the edges.
Parallel rays are bent **away from the principal axis**, so they **diverge**.
The principal focus is the point from which the diverging rays **appear to come**; it is found by drawing dotted construction lines backwards.
A concave lens always forms a **virtual, upright, diminished** image, whatever the object distance.
Because the rays never actually meet, a concave lens can **never** form an image on a screen by itself.
Concave lenses are used in **spectacles to correct short sight** and in some cameras and optical instruments in combination with convex lenses.
core.p: A **concave lens** is thinner in the middle than at the edges. It is called a **diverging lens** because it spreads parallel rays of light apart. After passing through, the rays move away from the principal axis, but if you trace them backwards in straight lines they appear to come from one point on the incident side of the lens. That point is the principal focus of a concave lens, and it is a **virtual** focus because the light does not actually pass through it.

bullets: **Principal axis**: the line through the centre of the lens, at 90 degrees to the lens.
**Principal focus**: the point where rays hitting the lens **parallel to the axis** meet (convex lens) or appear to come from (concave lens).
**Focal length**: the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
Every lens has a principal focus on **each side**; in diagrams you mark both as F, and often mark 2F (twice the focal length) as well.
A lens with a **short focal length** bends light strongly (powerful lens); a long focal length means weak bending.
Rays from a point on a very **distant object** are effectively parallel, so a convex lens focuses them at the principal focus; this is a simple way to measure the focal length of a lens.
core.h: Principal axis, principal focus and focal length
core.p: Three key terms describe the geometry of every lens diagram. The **principal axis** is the straight line that passes through the centre of the lens at right angles to it. The **principal focus** (focal point, F) is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (convex) or appear to diverge from (concave). The **focal length** is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus. These definitions are asked directly in short-answer questions, so learn them word for word.

bullets: **Real image**: formed where refracted rays actually meet; can be captured on a screen; always **inverted** for a single convex lens.
**Virtual image**: formed where rays only **appear** to come from when traced backwards; cannot be put on a screen.
On a ray diagram, **real image rays are drawn as solid lines** meeting at the image; for a virtual image the construction lines traced backwards are **dotted**.
A virtual image formed by a convex lens is on the **same side of the lens as the object**, upright and magnified.
The image is described using three pairs of words: **real or virtual**, **upright or inverted**, **magnified, same size or diminished**.
Cameras and projectors use **real** images; magnifying glasses use **virtual** images.
core.p: The type of image formed is one of the most important things to describe. A **real image** is formed when light rays actually **converge** and meet at a point; because the light really arrives there, the image can be **projected onto a screen**. A **virtual image** is formed when the rays are **diverging** after the lens, so they never meet, but when you look through the lens your brain traces them back in straight lines to where they appear to have come from. A virtual image **cannot be projected onto a screen**. Plane mirror images are also virtual.

bullets: Ray 1: from the top of the object, **parallel to the principal axis**, to the lens, then bends and goes **through the principal focus F** on the other side.
Ray 2: from the top of the object, **straight through the centre of the lens** with no change in direction.
The rays cross **between F and 2F** on the far side: draw the image as an arrow from the axis up/down to that crossing point.
Image properties: **real, inverted, diminished** (smaller than the object).
Because the image is real you could place a screen at that position and see it.
Used in **cameras** and in the **human eye** (the image on the retina is real, inverted and diminished; the brain interprets it the right way up).
core.p: When the object is **further from the lens than twice the focal length (beyond 2F)**, the lens forms a real image between F and 2F on the opposite side of the lens. The image is inverted and smaller than the object. This is how a **camera** works: a distant object is imaged as a small, inverted real image on the sensor or film. To draw it, you need two rays from the top of the object. The first travels parallel to the principal axis, bends at the lens and passes through the principal focus on the far side. The second travels straight through the centre of the lens without bending. Where the two rays cross is the top of the image.

bullets: Same construction rays: parallel ray through F and centre ray straight through.
The rays cross at a point **beyond 2F** on the far side of the lens.
Image properties: **real, inverted, magnified**.
If the object is exactly at **2F**, the image is also at 2F, **real, inverted and the same size** as the object.
Moving the object closer to F pushes the image further away and makes it bigger.
If the object is exactly at **F**, the refracted rays emerge **parallel**, so they never meet and **no image** is formed (the image is at infinity).
core.h: Convex lens: object between F and 2F
core.p: When the object is **between F and 2F** from the lens, the image forms **beyond 2F** on the far side, and it is **real, inverted and magnified**. The ray diagram is drawn using exactly the same two rays, but because the object is closer, the refracted rays meet further away and the image is larger. This is how a **projector** works: a small bright slide or screen, placed just beyond the focal length, is projected as a large inverted image on a distant screen, which is why slides are put into projectors upside down.

bullets: Draw ray 1 parallel to the axis, bending through F on the far side; draw ray 2 straight through the centre.
The two refracted rays **diverge**, so extend them **backwards as dotted lines** until they cross; the crossing point is the top of the virtual image.
Image properties: **virtual, upright, magnified**, on the **same side** as the object.
The virtual image is **further from the lens than the object**, which is why it appears bigger.
You cannot catch this image on a screen because no light actually arrives there.
This is the only arrangement with a convex lens that gives an **upright** image.
core.h: Convex lens: object closer than F (magnifying glass)
core.p: If the object is **between the lens and the principal focus (closer than F)**, the rays leaving the lens are still spreading out (diverging), though less than before. They cannot meet, so no real image forms. Instead, tracing the refracted rays backwards with dotted lines shows where they appear to come from: this is a **virtual image**, on the same side of the lens as the object, **upright and magnified**. This is how a **magnifying glass** works. You look through the lens and see a larger, upright image behind the object.

bullets: Ray 1: parallel to the axis, then bends **away from the axis** along a line that **appears to come from F** (the focus on the same side as the object); draw the back-tracing line dotted.
Ray 2: through the centre of the lens, **undeviated**.
The image is where the dotted back-traced line from ray 1 meets ray 2.
Image properties for any object position: **virtual, upright, diminished**.
The image is between the object and the lens and appears **closer** than the object.
A concave lens is useful in **short-sight glasses** because it makes the image appear closer so the weak eye can focus it.
core.p: The ray diagram for a concave lens uses the same two rays, but the first ray is bent so that it diverges. A ray from the top of the object travelling parallel to the axis is refracted so that it **appears to have come from the principal focus on the object side**. A ray through the centre goes straight on. The two refracted rays diverge so they never cross; the dotted lines traced backwards do cross, and the crossing point is the top of a **virtual, upright, diminished image** that sits closer to the lens than the object, on the same side. This is true at **every object distance**.

bullets: Equation: **magnification = image height / object height**.
Rearrangements: image height = magnification x object height; object height = image height / magnification.
**Always use the same units** for both heights (for example both in mm) before dividing; convert cm to mm by multiplying by 10.
Magnification **> 1**: magnified; **= 1**: same size; **< 1** (a fraction or decimal): diminished.
The answer is a **plain number with no unit** (do not write 'cm' or 'mm' after it).
Magnification can also be found from a ray diagram by measuring the image height and object height with a ruler.
core.p: **Magnification** tells you how much bigger or smaller the image is compared with the object. It is calculated as the image height divided by the object height. Because both heights are lengths measured in the same units, the units cancel and **magnification has no unit**. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object (magnified); exactly 1 means the same size; less than 1 means the image is smaller (diminished). Examiners expect you to give the equation in words, substitute, and, if the question gives different units, convert them first.

bullets: Draw the **principal axis** and a straight vertical line for the lens (a lens symbol with arrow heads is also fine).
Mark the **principal foci F** at equal distances either side of the lens using the scale given.
Draw the object as an arrow, base on the axis.
Draw ray 1 **parallel to the axis**, bent at the lens line to pass through F (convex) or to look as though it came from F (concave).
Draw ray 2 **through the centre of the lens** in a straight line.
**Dotted lines** for any construction that is not a real ray, and **arrowheads** on all rays.
Mark the **image** where the rays (or their dotted extensions) meet, draw it as an arrow from the axis, and **label** it; then state real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished.
Bend rays **at the lens line** (not at the curved edges) and keep the object, image and foci on a sensible scale.
core.h: How to draw a ray diagram (examiner checklist)
core.p: Ray diagrams are skills questions, and marks are given for specific features, so follow the same routine every time. Use a **sharp pencil and a ruler**, draw the lens as a vertical line with the principal axis horizontal, and mark F on both sides (and 2F if told). Draw the object as an upright arrow standing on the axis at the stated distance. Then add the two construction rays from the top of the object, finishing with arrows on every ray to show the direction light travels.

bullets: **Camera**: object beyond 2F, real, inverted, diminished image on a sensor.
**Projector**: object between F and 2F, real, inverted, magnified image on a screen.
**Magnifying glass**: object within F, virtual, upright, magnified image.
**Eye**: convex lens plus cornea focus a real inverted image on the retina; ciliary muscles change the lens shape to focus.
**Short sight (myopia)**: image forms in front of the retina; corrected with a **concave** lens to diverge the light slightly.
**Long sight (hypermetropia)**: image forms behind the retina; corrected with a **convex** lens to converge the light.
Link to **EM waves**: the lens bends visible light; other wavelengths are bent by different amounts because refraction depends on wavelength.
Link to **waves**: refraction depends on a change in wave speed, which depends on the medium.
core.h: Linking ideas: cameras, eye, projector and magnifier
core.p: The same convex lens can behave very differently depending on where the object is, which is why one topic explains many devices. A **camera** forms a small real inverted image of a distant object; a **projector** forms a large real inverted image of a nearby slide; a **magnifying glass** gives a large virtual upright image when the object is closer than the focal length. The **human eye** has a convex lens that focuses a real, inverted, diminished image of the world onto the retina. Short-sighted and long-sighted eyes are corrected with concave and convex lenses respectively. Applying the rules to a device is a common higher-mark question.

exam: **Describe an image (3 marks)**: give the three properties, e.g. 'real, inverted and diminished'; one mark each.

**Ray diagram (3 to 4 marks)**: 1 mark ray parallel to axis refracted through F, 1 mark ray through centre of lens undeviated, 1 mark image drawn correctly where rays meet, 1 mark for arrows or labelling.
Use a **ruler and sharp pencil** and the scale given on the grid; examiners allow about half a small square tolerance.
**Magnification calculation (2 to 3 marks)**: write the equation, substitute with the **same units**, give the answer with no unit; 1 mark for the equation or substitution, 1 for the answer.
**Command word 'Explain' (2 to 4 marks)**: say refraction, say what the lens does to the rays (converges/diverges) and link to the image formed.
**Compare convex and concave (4 marks)**: shape, effect on parallel rays, real or virtual image possible, example use.
**Which lens? questions**: convex converges and can form real images; concave only forms virtual images.
**Virtual image marks**: say 'cannot be projected onto a screen' or 'rays only appear to come from' to earn the mark.
**Camera/projector/magnifier questions**: link the object position (beyond 2F, between F and 2F, inside F) to the image type.
**Draw dotted lines** for rays traced backwards and say so if asked.
**Check the units** in measured heights from a diagram: measure with a ruler in mm, then divide.

mistakes.r: Size depends on object position: beyond 2F the image is diminished, at 2F it is the same size, between F and 2F it is magnified.
mistakes.w: Says a convex lens always makes images bigger.

mistakes.r: In a ray diagram, bend the ray once at the vertical line through the centre of the lens.
mistakes.w: Draws the ray bending at the curved edges of the lens.

mistakes.r: Real rays are solid with arrowheads; only construction lines that trace rays backwards are dotted.
mistakes.w: Forgets arrowheads on rays or draws rays as dotted lines.

mistakes.r: Magnification has no unit because it is a ratio of two lengths.
mistakes.w: Writes magnification with a unit, such as 3 cm.

mistakes.r: Convert both heights to the same unit first, then divide.
mistakes.w: Divides image height in mm by object height in cm without converting.

mistakes.r: A virtual image is formed where rays appear to come from when traced backwards; it cannot be projected onto a screen.
mistakes.w: Says a virtual image is 'not there' or is 'a reflection'.

mistakes.r: A concave lens makes parallel rays diverge; its principal focus is the point they appear to come from.
mistakes.w: Says the concave lens brings light to a focus.

mistakes.r: The ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on; a ray parallel to the axis passes through F after the lens.
mistakes.w: Says a ray through the principal focus goes straight through the lens.

mistakes.r: Describe the image fully: real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished, plus its position.
mistakes.w: Writes 'upside down' only, without saying real or virtual and magnified or diminished.

summary: The specification asks you to describe how convex and concave lenses refract light, to draw ray diagrams for each, to state whether the image is real or virtual, upright or inverted, and magnified or diminished, and to calculate magnification. It matters because the same ideas explain cameras, projectors, magnifying glasses and the human eye.

terms.d: A piece of transparent material with curved surfaces that refracts light to form an image.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays of light together at a principal focus.
A lens that is thinner in the middle and spreads parallel rays of light apart.
The line through the centre of a lens at right angles to the lens.
The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (convex) or appear to come from (concave) after passing through the lens.
The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in speed.
An image formed where light rays actually meet; it can be projected onto a screen.
An image formed where light rays only appear to come from when traced backwards; it cannot be projected onto a screen.
image height divided by object height; it has no unit.
An image that is upside down compared with the object.
An image that is the same way up as the object.
An image that is smaller than the object (magnification less than 1).
An image that is larger than the object (magnification greater than 1).
A scale drawing that uses rays to find the position, size and type of image formed by a lens.
A point on the principal axis at a distance twice the focal length from the lens.

worked.q: An object is 2.0 cm tall. A convex lens forms an image that is 7.0 cm tall. Calculate the magnification. (2 marks)
steps: Both heights are in cm, so no conversion needed.

worked.q: A magnifying glass has a magnification of 4. The object is 1.5 mm tall. Calculate the height of the image in mm. (2 marks)
steps: Rearrange: image height = magnification x object height.

worked.ans: 0.002 (no unit); the image is much smaller than the object, so it is diminished.
worked.q: A photo of a tree is 24 mm tall on the camera sensor. The tree is 12 m tall. Calculate the magnification. (3 marks)
steps: Convert tree height to mm: 12 m = 12 000 mm.
